root.note: skholē first meant ‘free time’, then what you do with it: talking, thinking, listening to a teacher.

stages.meaning: a place where children go to learn

history: School is a surprising word, because it began as the opposite of work. In ancient Greek, skholē meant ‘free time, leisure’. Rich Greeks used their free time to talk and think, so skholē came to mean ‘a discussion’, then ‘a lecture’, and finally ‘a place where people learn’. The Romans borrowed it as schola, and the Anglo-Saxons took scōl from Latin when Christian monks started schools in England. German Schule, French école and Spanish escuela all come from the same Latin word. A school of fish is a different word: it comes from Dutch school, ‘a group’, and is related to shoal.
historyEinfach: School is a Greek word. But in Greek, skholē meant ‘free time’! In their free time, rich people talked and learned. So the word changed: it became ‘a place where you learn’. The Romans said schola. The English said scōl, and later school.

elsewhere.text: Modern Greek still has the old word: σχολείο is a school, and σχολή is a faculty at a university. The ‘free time’ meaning is gone; for that, Greek says ελεύθερος χρόνος.
Spanish escuela and French école come from Latin schola. Spanish added an e- in front, as it does in many words that once began with s + consonant: escuela, estudiante, España.
